title: We can't have children
seoTitle: Infertility and Faith: When You Can't Have Children
description: When you can't have children: the monthly grief, the strain on a marriage, what the Bible says, what to do this week, and how to help a friend.
summary: For the ache of an empty nursery and a long wait, with Hannah's honesty and without platitudes.
askedAs: what does the Bible say about infertility
answer: You want a child, and month after month the answer has been no. Maybe you've been trying for a year, or through years of tests and treatments, or you lost a pregnancy and the child you'd already begun to love. It's a grief with no funeral, and it starts over every few weeks, usually in private, while friends announce pregnancies and relatives ask when you're going to start a family. Your longing isn't selfish, and your empty arms are not God's verdict on your faith or your worth. Nothing about treatment or adoption has to be decided tonight. Tell one person the truth about how hard this has been, and if you're married, start with your spouse.
happening:
Infertility can arrive as one hard diagnosis, but for many it's a long accumulation of small disappointments: a couple of weeks each month of hope you promised yourself you wouldn't feel, then a day when it ends again, often alone, before work. The calendar starts to run your life, and even intimacy can turn into a schedule. There are tests, waiting rooms, injections, and bills, and each result can feel like a verdict. Meanwhile the announcements keep coming, at Thanksgiving, in the group chat, at church, at the shower. You can love your friend and still be unable to hold her newborn this week. Feeling both doesn't make you a bad person.

Some of you have conceived, only to lose the pregnancy. A miscarriage is a real loss however early it came, and it's often grieved in near silence because so few people knew there was a child to lose.

Infertility also tests a marriage in new places. Husbands and wives often grieve differently: one wants to talk, the other wants to fix it or stop talking about it. One of you may be ready for the next treatment while the other is worn out. If the cause has been traced to one of you, that spouse may carry a private shame, and many men hide this grief as if it were a failure of manhood.

Each common explanation holds something true. Doctors will tell you infertility is a medical condition, not a moral one, with causes in the man, the woman, or both, and sometimes none that tests can find, and that treatment helps many couples. That lifts an old shame. Counselors will tell you this is real grief even with no body to bury, and they're right. Friends at church will say God has a plan, and Scripture does teach that nothing is outside his hand. But medicine can turn your body into a project, the language of grief can name the loss without giving you anywhere to take it, and talk of a plan can sound like a promise that faith ends in a baby once you pass the test.

scripture.intro: Scripture doesn't treat childlessness as a small sorrow. Its story keeps returning to women who waited and husbands who prayed or said the wrong thing, and it keeps their anguish on the page. It also refuses to call their empty arms a punishment. Read these slowly, one a day if that's all you can manage.

passages.text: And this went on year after year. Whenever Hannah went up to the house of the LORD, her rival taunted her until she wept and would not eat. “Hannah, why are you crying?” her husband Elkanah asked. “Why won’t you eat? Why is your heart so grieved? Am I not better to you than ten sons?” ... In her bitter distress, Hannah prayed to the LORD and wept with many tears. ... “No, my lord,” Hannah replied. “I am a woman oppressed in spirit. I have not had any wine or strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the LORD.
passages.reading: Hannah's story opens in a household where the other wife had children and Hannah had none, because “the LORD had closed her womb” (1 Samuel 1:5). The narrator doesn't explain that, and never calls it a punishment. Her husband loved her and asked a kind question that missed her completely. Then the priest saw her lips move without a sound and decided she was drunk; those of us who serve in churches still misread grief. Her face changed after she prayed, before anything had changed in her body (1 Samuel 1:18). She did bear a son, and Scripture doesn't promise you her ending. It shows you her God, who heard a prayer made mostly of tears.

passages.text: How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me? How long must I wrestle in my soul, with sorrow in my heart each day? How long will my enemy dominate me? Consider me and respond, O LORD my God. Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death, lest my enemy say, “I have overcome him,” and my foes rejoice when I fall. But I have trusted in Your loving devotion; my heart will rejoice in Your salvation. I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me.
passages.reading: This psalm bears David's name, and it asks *how long* four times before it asks for anything else, which is the question infertility asks every month. It accuses God of forgetting and of hiding his face, but it says all of it to God, which makes even the accusation a prayer. In the last two verses it turns to trust, though nothing in it says the trouble has lifted; the turn is a choice made in the dark. Some months you won't be able to pray those last two verses. Pray the first four verses honestly and stop there. This psalm is in your Bible for months like this one.

passages.text: When Rachel saw that she was not bearing any children for Jacob, she envied her sister. “Give me children, or I will die!” she said to Jacob. Jacob became angry with Rachel and said, “Am I in the place of God, who has withheld children from you?”
passages.reading: Rachel was the wife Jacob loved, and her sister Leah had just given him four sons (Genesis 29:31-35). The narrator names Rachel's envy and records her raw demand, and Jacob answers in anger with a sentence that's true about God and cruel at that moment. Both wound the other, and that's what infertility can do: put two people who love each other on opposite sides of the same grief. Envy is where the ache can turn hard. In the verses that follow, the rivalry runs through the names the sisters give their sons, and Rachel names one for having “wrestled with my sister and won” (Genesis 30:8). Bring that part to God too. Later, “God remembered Rachel. He listened to her” (Genesis 30:22). If Rachel's sentence has become more than a figure of speech for you, if you've had thoughts of not wanting to live, call or text 988 tonight.

passages.text: Both of them were righteous in the sight of God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and decrees of the Lord. But they had no children, because Elizabeth was barren, and they were both well along in years. ... After these days, his wife Elizabeth became pregnant and for five months remained in seclusion. She declared, “The Lord has done this for me. In these days He has shown me favor and taken away my disgrace among the people.”
passages.reading: Luke begins his story with an old priest and his wife, and before he tells you they had no children, he tells you they were righteous and blameless. Then comes the word *but*. He sets their faithfulness and their childlessness side by side so that no reader can blame the second on a lack of the first. When the promise of a son came, Zechariah couldn't believe it (Luke 1:18); long waiting does that to hope. When Elizabeth conceived, she spoke of “my disgrace among the people,” a shame others had laid on her, though in God's sight she had been righteous all along. What Luke settles is the verdict: their empty years were never a sign that God thought less of them, and neither are yours.

passages.text: And let the eunuch not say, “I am but a dry tree.” For this is what the LORD says: “To the eunuchs who keep My Sabbaths, who choose what pleases Me and hold fast to My covenant— I will give them, in My house and within My walls, a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters. I will give them an everlasting name that will not be cut off.
passages.reading: In Israel a man's name lived on through his children, and the law kept the eunuch out of the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1). Isaiah expects him to call himself a dry tree, words many childless people would recognize. God answers with a name “better than that of sons and daughters,” a place in his own house that will never be cut off. Centuries later, Luke tells of an Ethiopian eunuch riding home from Jerusalem, reading Isaiah at the line “Who can recount His descendants?” (Acts 8:33). A man who could have no descendants was reading about a Servant cut off without them, and Philip began there and told him about Jesus (Acts 8:35). The eunuch “went on his way rejoicing” (Acts 8:39). In the church, a person without children was never meant to be a guest.

whyHard:
Infertility is hard because the loss is real. But many people carry a second weight on top of it: the sense that they've failed at something everyone else manages without trying, or that God is keeping score. Some of that weight comes from the world we've built, and some of it was put there by the church.

The ancient world counted children as a family's future, its security in old age and the survival of its name, so childlessness brought shame along with sorrow. When Rachel's son was born she said, “God has taken away my shame” (Genesis 30:23). Scripture records that shame honestly, but it keeps taking the side of the shamed, Hannah over her rival and the eunuch over his own verdict on himself. And Jesus redrew the family: told that his mother and brothers were outside, he looked at the people around him and said, “Here are My mother and My brothers!” (Mark 3:34).

Our own era added a different weight. In 1960 the first birth control pill was approved in the United States, and in 1978 the first child conceived through IVF was born in England. Within a couple of generations, many of us learned to think of children as something we choose and schedule. Medicine has been a real mercy, and many families exist because of it. But when a pregnancy is supposed to be a decision, its failure feels like your failure, and when there is always one more test or one more cycle, a grief that might have been mourned becomes a project with no natural end. The longing is ancient. The expectation of control is new.

The church has its own part. Many congregations have made the family with children the picture of faithfulness, a good thing to honor and a hard thing to sit through when it isn't yours. In some churches the mothers stand to be applauded on Mother's Day, and couples without children hear in a hundred small ways that they're behind. I'm a pastor and the father of five sons, which puts me inside both the picture those Sundays celebrate and the indictment. Other churches say nothing about this grief at all. And some promise what God hasn't, that enough faith will open a womb, which turns a closed womb into the couple's fault. We meant to honor families, and we built rooms where a childless couple can feel like guests at someone else's celebration.

If you don't share my faith, you may think this is where it breaks: the Bible says the LORD closed Hannah's womb, and couples who pray for years hear nothing back. I came to faith from atheism, so I won't call that objection small. The Bible keeps Rachel's demand and Hannah's tears in plain view, and it never explains why one couple conceives and another doesn't. What it offers is a God who hears, a Savior who died without children of his own, and a family in which no one's name is cut off.

A child is a gift, never a payment for faith, and a church that treats childless people as unfinished has forgotten whose family it is.

thisWeek.intro: These steps won't give you a child, and they aren't meant to. They're small ways to keep the wait from swallowing everything else. Start with the first; if it's the only one you manage, that's enough.

steps.title: Say one true sentence
steps.body: Tell someone how this month really went: your spouse if you're married, or a friend who can keep a confidence. One sentence is enough, something like *I'm not okay this month.* If the two of you grieve differently, agree on a time to talk about it and a time to set it down, so it doesn't swallow every evening. Elkanah asked the wrong question (1 Samuel 1:8). Ask a better one: *How are you, really?*

steps.title: Pray like Hannah
steps.body: Find a place to be alone and tell God exactly what you want and how much it hurts; Hannah didn't tidy up her prayer first. If you can't find words, pray Psalm 13 aloud, as far as you honestly can. When even that is too much, the Spirit “intercedes for us with groans too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). Your groaning counts.

steps.title: Mark the hard days ahead
steps.body: Put the hard dates on your calendar now: Mother's Day and Father's Day, the shower you've been invited to, a due date that came and went, the anniversary of a loss. Decide ahead of time where you'll be and who will know. On Mother's Day you can stay home, or sit near the back beside someone who knows and leave when you need to. You can send a gift and a kind note instead of going to the shower; love doesn't require you to grieve in public.

steps.title: Decide your limits together
steps.body: If you're in treatment or thinking about it, talk through what you will and won't do before the next step: how many tries, how much money, what you believe about embryos, and what you'll do if this round fails. Write it down, and ask your doctor plain questions about costs and chances. If you can't agree, take it to a counselor or a pastor you both trust. Decide together in daylight, not alone in a clinic hallway.

steps.title: Make room for the life you have
steps.body: Waiting can put a whole life on hold: the trip you won't book in case you're pregnant, the job you won't take, the friends you've let drift. Choose one thing this month that belongs to the life you have now. Hope can keep its place without taking every room in the house.

moreHelp.body:
Infertility is a medical condition as well as a grief, so the first help is often a doctor. Doctors generally suggest an evaluation after a year of trying, or after six months if the woman is 35 or older. Ask that both of you be evaluated, since the cause can lie with either spouse. A specialist called a reproductive endocrinologist can explain options that may range from medicine or surgery to insemination or IVF.

The grief may need help too. A counselor who works with infertility or pregnancy loss can help you carry the monthly cycle of hope and loss, and help a husband and wife hear each other again. Ask your doctor or clinic for a referral, search your insurer's directory, or ask your pastor which counselors they trust. If you want a Christian counselor, ask for one, and either way confirm with your state's licensing board that they're licensed. If your marriage itself is in trouble, read [My marriage is falling apart](/help/marriage).
signs: Thoughts of ending your life or of not wanting to wake up. Call or text 988 now, or call 911 if you're in danger.
Heavy bleeding, severe pain, fever, or fainting in pregnancy or after a loss or procedure. Call your doctor now, or 911 if it's severe.
Sadness that hasn't lifted for weeks, or you've stopped sleeping, eating, or working. See a doctor or a counselor.
You can't talk about it without blaming each other, or one of you has gone silent for months. See a counselor together, if you're safe with each other.
You've become afraid of your spouse, or the blame has turned into threats or control. Call the Domestic Violence Hotline at the end of this page, or 911 if you're in danger.
You're considering adoption, a donor, or a surrogate. Talk to a lawyer who knows your state's family law before you sign anything.
moreHelp.firstCall: To a doctor: *We've been trying to get pregnant for more than a year. What tests should both of us have, and what will they cost?* To a counselor: *The monthly disappointment is wearing us down, and we've started taking it out on each other.* Ask whether they're licensed in your state, whether they've worked with infertility or pregnancy loss, what they charge, and whether they take your insurance. If your faith matters, say so: *I'm a Christian, and I'd like that to be welcome here.*
moreHelp.cost: Fertility treatment can be expensive, and coverage depends on your state and plan, so ask your insurer exactly what's covered and get a written estimate from the clinic that includes medications. For counseling, an employee assistance program may cover a few sessions, and community mental health centers and university training clinics often charge on a sliding scale. Ask your clinic about support groups for infertility or pregnancy loss, and whether a counselor or a volunteer leads them. If the cost is crushing you, tell your pastor; some churches keep a fund for needs like this.

helping.body:
If someone you love can't have children, believe them and stay close. Don't offer medical tips, adoption stories, or reasons; ask how they're doing this month, and listen. Men grieve this too, so ask the husband, not only the wife. If you're pregnant, tell your friend privately, in a message they can read alone, before the news goes public, so they don't have to arrange their face in front of a crowd. Would-be grandparents grieve as well, but don't add your disappointment to your children's.

Pastors, this includes us. If you honor mothers or fathers on their day, pray in the same breath for those who long to be parents, those who have lost children, and those whose parents are gone or were hard to love. At a baby dedication, pray for the families still waiting. Never ask the church to pray for a couple to conceive without their permission, and never ask anyone when they're going to start a family.
say: I'm so sorry. That sounds really hard.
How are you doing this month, really?
You don't have to come to the shower. I'll understand.
I'm praying for you both, and I'll keep asking.
Mother's Day is coming. Do you want company, or a call afterward?
dontSay: Just relax and it will happen.
It must not be God's timing yet.
My cousin got pregnant right after she stopped trying.
At least you have your freedom.
So when are you two having kids?
helping.next: Mark the hard days they've told you about in your calendar and check in on them. Keep inviting them, even when they say no. If they talk about not wanting to live, ask plainly whether they're thinking about suicide; asking won't put the idea in their head. Help them call or text 988, or call 911 if they're in danger. If they fear their spouse, ask how it's safe to reach them, since phones can be watched, and point them to the Domestic Violence Hotline at the end of this page.

prayer:
Lord, you heard Hannah when her lips moved and no sound came out. Hear me now, because I'm tired of praying the same prayer.

We want a child. Every month I let myself hope, and every month it ends, and I don't know how many more times I can do this. Some days I'm angry with you. Some days I can't look at a stroller. Forgive me where the ache has turned into envy, and don't let it make me hard.

Don't let this grief make strangers of us in our own house. Give us wisdom about what to do next, and the courage to stop if that time comes.

You know every child we've hoped for and every loss no one else saw. My groaning is not hidden from you. When I can't pray, let your Spirit pray for me. Give me a name in your house that nothing can cut off, and hold on to me until I can trust you again. Amen.

faq.q: Is infertility a punishment from God?
faq.a: Scripture gives you no reason to read your own childlessness that way. Luke calls Zechariah and Elizabeth “righteous in the sight of God,” then adds, “But they had no children” (Luke 1:6-7). When the disciples assumed a man's blindness was punishment for sin, Jesus answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3). It's true that the Bible sometimes names childlessness as a judgment, and when it does, it says so and gives the reason (Genesis 20:18). The law also promised a faithful Israel that “there will be no barren man or woman” among them (Deuteronomy 7:14), yet Elizabeth kept that law blamelessly and still waited into old age. No one may read a hidden sin off an empty nursery. If something in your past haunts you anyway, bring it to God by name: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9), and “there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

faq.q: Does God promise a baby if I have enough faith?
faq.a: No one can promise you that, and anyone who does is promising more than God has. Psalm 113 praises the God who “settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother to her children” (Psalm 113:9). It's a hymn about the kind of God he is, one who stoops to lift the low, and it sits in the same Bible as Hannah's years of prayer. Hebrews does say Sarah conceived by faith, but she was trusting a son God had specifically promised (Genesis 18:10; Hebrews 11:11), and the same chapter honors people who “died in faith, without having received the things they were promised” (Hebrews 11:13). The teaching that enough faith will open your womb is a form of the prosperity gospel, and it wounds twice: no child, and then the blame. Pray as boldly as Hannah did. Your faith isn't measured by the answer.

faq.q: We lost a pregnancy. Why does it hurt this much?
faq.a: Because you lost a child you had already begun to love, and love doesn't wait for a due date. However early the loss came, that child was real, and so is your grief. Some parents grieve hard and some are surprised by what they feel; neither is a failure of love. You're allowed to mourn: to name the baby, to mark the date, to ask your church to pray with you. Psalm 139 praises the God who “knit me together in my mother’s womb” (Psalm 139:13), and no child is hidden from him, however brief their life. See your doctor for your body's sake, and a counselor if the sadness won't lift. Husbands grieve these losses too, often quietly. There's more in [Miscarriage and Pregnancy Loss](/wisdom/miscarriage).

Faithful Christians disagree, and it divides churches, not the faith. The Catholic Church teaches, and some Protestants agree, that a child should be conceived only through the marital act of husband and wife, who “will become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24), so that a child is received as a gift, never produced. It welcomes treatment that helps the body conceive but holds IVF morally unacceptable, even with the couple's own egg and sperm, and donors and surrogates gravely wrong; it also teaches that a child is never owed, and that childless couples can give their love through adoption or service (Catechism 2375 to 2379). Many Protestants hold that a married couple may use IVF with their own egg and sperm, receiving medicine as a gift, if every embryo is treated as a child: “Your eyes saw my unformed body” (Psalm 139:16). So they create no more embryos than they will carry, and discard none. Others also accept donated eggs, sperm, or embryos, holding that such a child is welcomed much as an adopted child is, and that a donated embryo carried to birth is a life received, not lost. Talk it through with your pastor and doctor before you begin.

Adoption is beautiful, and it sits close to the heart of the gospel: God sent his Son “that we might receive our adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:5). But it's a calling for some, not a cure for infertility. It doesn't erase the grief for the child you couldn't conceive, and no child should be asked to fill that space. Adopted children carry losses of their own, and they deserve parents who have grieved theirs. If you're drawn to it, take your time, listen to adoptive families and adult adoptees, and talk with a licensed agency and an attorney. If you aren't drawn to it, that isn't selfishness, and your life isn't on hold without it. Some find a different calling in foster care or in mentoring a child who needs a steady adult.

slots.note: James has five sons. The section says only that he is a pastor and the father of five sons, inside both the picture that family-centered Sundays celebrate and the indictment. In his own words, he could say how he holds that fact before readers who cannot have children, and anything about waiting, infertility, or pregnancy loss in his own family that he chooses to share. Nothing is assumed about his family's story; the section stands without it.

Is IVF wrong for Christians: where James lands, in his own words, on IVF with a couple's own egg and sperm, on donors and surrogacy, and on frozen embryos, and the strongest objection he hasn't fully answered (no denominational label; no page speaks for his tradition). The answer gives three positions, each in a form its defenders would sign: the Catholic teaching, with the Protestants who share it (Genesis 2:24; a child received as a gift, never owed); the conditional acceptance many Protestants hold (Psalm 139:16; every embryo treated as a child); and the wider acceptance of donated eggs, sperm, or embryos, reasoned from adoption. It deliberately does not land.

James came to faith from atheism. Beside the paragraph that answers the skeptic, he could add in his own words what he once made of unanswered longing and of a God the Bible says opens and closes wombs. The paragraph says only that he came to faith from atheism.

If James wishes: how First Baptist Church of Fenton handles Mother's Day, Father's Day, and baby dedications for those who are waiting or grieving, and any infertility or pregnancy-loss support groups, Christian counselors, or adoption agencies near Fenton he trusts enough to name. Only from James; nothing about his church's practice has been described.

sources.claim: Infertility means not being able to get pregnant after one year of trying, or after six months if a woman is 35 or older (the page says only that doctors generally suggest an evaluation at those points).
sources.cite: Office on Women's Health, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Infertility (confirmed through search excerpts; direct fetches were blocked; re-open before release).

sources.claim: Infertility can arise in men or women; when no cause can be found it is diagnosed as unexplained; treatments range from medication and surgery to assisted reproductive technology such as donor insemination and in vitro fertilization.
sources.cite: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD), What infertility treatments are available? and the NICHD infertility fact sheet (search excerpts; re-open before release).

sources.claim: A reproductive endocrinologist is an obstetrician-gynecologist with additional fellowship training in reproductive endocrinology and infertility.
sources.cite: American Society for Reproductive Medicine, ReproductiveFacts.org, SART Fertility Experts: What Is an REI? (search excerpts; re-open before release).

sources.claim: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Enovid, the first birth control pill, for contraceptive use in 1960.
sources.cite: PBS, American Experience, The FDA Approves the Pill (search excerpts; re-open before release).

sources.claim: Louise Brown, the first person born after conception by in vitro fertilization, was born on July 25, 1978, in Oldham, England.
sources.cite: Wikipedia, Louise Brown; consistent with Fertility and Sterility, First in vitro fertilization baby: this is how it happened (search excerpts; re-open before release).

sources.claim: The Catechism encourages research aimed at reducing sterility (2375), calls techniques involving a donor or surrogate gravely immoral (2376), holds that techniques involving only the married couple remain morally unacceptable (2377), teaches that a child is not something owed but a gift (2378), and that childless spouses can express their generosity by adopting or serving others (2379).
sources.cite: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section Two, Chapter Two, Article 6, The Gift of a Child (paragraphs confirmed through search excerpts; re-open before release).

sources.claim: Many evangelicals accept IVF for a married couple only when the embryos come from the couple's own egg and sperm and no embryos are frozen or discarded. (The page states this position without any survey figure.)
sources.cite: Christianity Today, How IVF Made Its Way into Evangelical Pro-Life Debates (January 2024) (search excerpts; re-open before release).

sources.claim: Protestant positions on IVF vary and are sometimes unclear, and some Protestants argue against IVF altogether.
sources.cite: Canopy Forum (Center for the Study of Law and Religion, Emory University), Whittney Barth, What Do Protestants Believe about In Vitro Fertilization? It's Complicated (October 2024); for a Protestant case against IVF, Matthew Lee Anderson, The Biblical Case Against IVF, First Things (2021) (search excerpts; re-open before release).

sources.claim: Whether insurance covers infertility treatment depends on the state and the plan: some states require certain plans to cover some infertility care, with differing scope, and state mandates do not reach self-funded employer plans.
sources.cite: KFF, Mandated Coverage of Infertility Treatment, and Coverage and Use of Fertility Services in the U.S. (search excerpts; re-open before release).

sources.claim: Asking someone directly whether they are thinking about suicide does not increase suicidal thoughts or behavior.
sources.cite: National Institute of Mental Health, 5 Action Steps to Help Someone Having Thoughts of Suicide.

sources.claim: A partner may monitor a survivor's phone and devices, so a safer device or a safe way of contact matters.
sources.cite: National Domestic Violence Hotline, Internet Safety for Survivors.

reviewed.notes: Second pass (editor), 2026-10-01; supersedes the writer's self-check. Validator clean (node scripts/validate-needs.mjs infertility, 4,306 words) and the CarePage render test passes. Truth: every setting re-read in the BSB with --verses (1 Samuel 1:1-28; Genesis 29:31 to 30:24; Psalm 13; Luke 1:5-25; Isaiah 56:1-8 with Deuteronomy 23:1; Acts 8:26-39 with Isaiah 53:8; Mark 3:31-35; Psalm 113; Hebrews 11:8-13 with Genesis 18:10-14; John 9:1-3; Genesis 20:17-18; Deuteronomy 7:12-15; Leviticus 20:20-21; Psalm 139:13-16; Romans 8:1). The punishment answer said Scripture goes out of its way to say so, but Leviticus 20:20-21 names childlessness as a penalty, and the old answer called Genesis 20:18 judgment where the text says on account of Sarah; it now concedes that the Bible sometimes names childlessness as a judgment and then says so and gives the reason, sets Deuteronomy 7:14 beside Elizabeth's blameless waiting (so no one may read a hidden sin off an empty nursery), and replaces the line that framed confession around a possible payment with 1 John 1:9 and Romans 8:1. The faith answer now meets Hebrews 11:11 (Sarah conceived by faith in a son God had specifically promised, Genesis 18:10) before Hebrews 11:13, and calls faith-for-a-child a form of the prosperity gospel. Genesis 30:8: the writer's summary (the sisters made their children a contest) is now framed as a summary with its evidence, Rachel naming a son for having wrestled with her sister and won; the narrator names Rachel's envy, so without comment was cut. Luke's story, not his Gospel, opens with Zechariah (1:1-4 is a preface); Elizabeth called what she carried (ambiguous, since she was pregnant) now reads that she spoke of her disgrace when she conceived, and Zechariah's unbelief comes first, as in the text. Isaiah 56:3 tells the eunuch not to call himself a dry tree, so the reading says Isaiah expects him to; the Servant of Isaiah 53:8 is cut off without descendants (53:10 promises offspring, so with none was loose). Outside claims (confirmed only through search excerpts) kept only where ordinary and certain: the evaluation guideline (a year, or six months at 35 or older), causes in either spouse or none found, the reproductive endocrinologist, the pill approved in the United States in 1960, the first IVF birth in England in 1978, and Catechism 2375 to 2379.
